title: Revolution for Everyone?
sub: Grades 5–8 · Social Studies · Change, reform and who it reached

hero.credit: *The Centre Refreshment Room, opened 1868.* Photograph, late 1860s. V&A E.655-2009. © Victoria and Albert Museum, London

objective: Students will read the exhibition’s two posters as a historical account of Victorian Britain (1837–1901). They will sort evidence of **change** — railways, the telegraph, the Great Exhibition, the V&A, the 1842 coal mines law, the revival of Christmas — from evidence of **continuity**: long working hours, class divisions and urban challenges. Asking *for whom?* of each change, they will judge how far the age was revolutionary for everyone.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: Every account of the past chooses what to put first. Asking *for whom?* is how historians test a story of progress, in Victorian Britain and today.

materials: Both posters, on screen or in the exhibition; the evidence chart on page 3, projected or printed
connection: **Visit the exhibition:** walk poster 1, then poster 2, and list every change each names. In the *Inventions Workshop,* the railway bench shows towns giving up their own time for London’s; in *Dickens’ Christmas Parlour,* poster 2’s account of Christmas opens part by part.

steps.title: Whose Britain?
script: Show the court dress from poster 1 and read the poster’s first sentence: *“Victorian Britain was a time of innovation, fashion, culture, and the birth of one of the most iconic museums in the world today!”* Tell students the dress was made in the 1860s; its embroidered train is 11 feet long, and young women practiced for hours to curtsey and walk backward in a dress like it before being presented at court. Ask: *“Whose Victorian Britain is this? Who might be missing from it?”*

steps.purpose: Set out what the posters say changed in Victorian Britain.
students: Name one change of each kind.

steps.title: What persisted
script: Then put up the one sentence in poster 1 about what did not change: *“Social reform improved conditions for workers, while class divisions and urban challenges persisted.”* Ask: *what does* persisted *mean? How much space does the poster give it, compared with the inventions and the museum?*

screen.text: Social reform improved conditions for workers, while class divisions and urban challenges persisted.

steps.purpose: Find the sentence where the poster admits the limits of progress.
students: Why might a poster give this only one sentence?

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students choose a handout. All three levels work from the same evidence, taken from the two posters.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Sort eight pieces of evidence into *changed for working people* and *stayed hard*; place five events on a timeline; answer the question with a sentence frame.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Read poster 1 as a source: what it puts first and what it passes over. Chart change and continuity, with *for whom?*, then write a claim paragraph.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Judge the 1842 law by its limits; question what the poster leaves unsaid; write an argument on *revolutionary for whom?* that answers an objection.

steps.purpose: Weigh the evidence of change and continuity at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. All three use the same evidence from the two posters.

steps.title: The evidence
script: Project the evidence chart. Each group chooses one line, calls it *change* or *continuity*, and says for whom. Close on poster 1’s title: *was Victorian Britain revolutionary for everyone?* Let a Red Level student give the strongest objection.

cells: The Victorian era: the reign of Queen Victoria. Rapid industrial growth made Britain a global superpower with an expanding empire.
The first commercially successful use of Cooke and Wheatstone’s electric telegraph anywhere in the world, on a London railway.

A report on children working in coal mines shocked the public. A new law made it illegal for women and girls, or boys under ten, to work underground. With one inspector for the whole country it was hard to enforce: a first step.
The Great Exhibition in the Crystal Palace, Hyde Park: about six million visitors, a third of Britain’s population.

The V&A is founded, “a schoolroom for everyone” in the words of its first director, Henry Cole. Gas lighting let its galleries open on winter evenings, so working people could visit after a day’s work.
Nearly every town has switched from its own Sun time to “railway time.”

At the start of the century Christmas was hardly celebrated: many businesses did not treat it as a holiday, and long hours left workers little time. The new railways let people who had moved to the cities travel home for Christmas.
Christmas had become the biggest celebration of the year in Britain.

steps.purpose: Pull the evidence together, and test the poster’s word *revolutionary*.
students: Pick one piece of evidence: change or continuity?
